"Ye" as in "Ye Olde" was never pronounced like a Y, the "Y" was actually a placeholder for the letter "thorn", which makes the "th" sound.

True, but I'm not going to let reality get in the way of a joke.

Old and Middle English had quite a few letters that are no longer used today, there's thorn (þ) and eth (ð) which were used for the th sounds, wynn (ƿ) which was used for the w sound, ȝ (yogh) which has many pronunciations ranging from a hard g sound, a w sound, a y sound and the sound of ch in Scottish "loch", and, finally, ash (æ) which represented a sound like the a in "cat" in American English.

Thorn and eth are still used today in Icelandic and ash is still occasionally used in modern English and French for Latin and Greek borrowings (like "encyclopædia") and is used in Icelandic, Faroese, Danish and Norwegian to represent various sounds.
I would've been illiterate in the middle ages, between this and Latin.

Old English spelling was actually a lot more phonetic than Modern English, and Middle English didn't have a standard orthography so you could've literally spelt words however you wanted. Most people were illiterate, though, because you had to be rich to be educated.
It's context like this that makes the antics of spelling reformers amusing. Spelling standardization and simplification is partly what made this language so messy and seemingly inconsistent.
Standardisation, yes, I wouldn't say simplification, though.

I guess it could be seen as making spelling more complex, but my thought was that the two different letters for similar sounds (thorn and eth, for voiced and voiceless th sound) were merged into one written form (th).

I think that was done more for the ease of the printing press in Europe, since they didn't have characters for thorn or eth, or maybe that spelling was introduced by the French, since English stopped being a written language after the Norman Conquest. Thorn and eth actually stuck around into Middle English, where eth was eventually displaced by thorn and I guess the people at the printing press thought thorn looked like a Y? I believe that <d> and <th> were actually used before thorn and eth, so I suppose that's why people started to use <th>, with analogy to Latin's <th>, which was used to transliterate Greek <θ>, which has come to be pronounced the same as English's voiceless <th> in Modern Greek.
